newsitem.title: RWANDA: The dispossessed return to Rwanda, in hope.
newsitem.headline: The dispossessed return to Rwanda, in hope.

text.p: Each refugee heading home to Rwanda has a tale of exile and hopes for the future, some realistic and some testimony to a collective amnesia born of desperation.
Together they tell of a Hutu struggle to live. For some, the trek back home in a tide of humanity was at times more harrowing than their equally rapid flight to Zaire two-and-a-half years ago.

"God truly loves us," said 42-year-old Rose Dusabumwe, in tears on Monday as she was reunited in Rwanda with the husband and two sons she lost when her 14-year-old daughter collapsed in Zaire during the trek.
On Sunday, she had rested two steps from Rwanda, shielding her daughter from the rain and cursing the Hutu leaders who told the refugees to stay in Zaire and wasted their lives.
Hours later, aid workers drove them to a clinic in Rwanda.

"We are home. I have dreamed of this for two years...Being a refugee is nothing. You are always afraid and pushed around," she said after her husband, steering a cart full of belongings and bags she wove in the camp, caught up with her on Monday.
For others, marching back is almost the easiest part. There is safety in numbers and hope for the future, all worries momentarily set aside.
The refugees agree overall on what suddenly ended their mass exile last week in the volcanic wilderness of eastern Zaire.
"Our time in Zaire ran out," said potato farmer Jean-Marie Nitegeka, 35, eating plates of beans with his two wives and seven childen during a break from the line plodding eastwards.
"Our camps were attacked by rebels, the NGOs (independent aid agencies) stopped feeding us and our leaders fled. We realised we had nowhere else to go but home to live," he says.
"Before we left Mugunga camp on Friday we saw as many dead as there are stars in the heavens," he adds. Asked who killed them, he says he does not know because he hid in a ditch.

"The politicians, leaders, soldiers and Interahamwe (militia) with us told us it was not safe here. But it is," says Innocent Nkundabanga, a 47-year-old farmer walking with two of his children and worried for the other four and his wife lost in the crowd.

These are apparently not the mass killers of Rwanda's 1994 genocide. Tutsis and Hutus alike believe those murderers will not return to be accused by their former neighbours. These are the innocent, or those who perhaps at most pointed out Tutsi homes.
But ask Nitegeka, and his friend Alphonse, wearing a red, American work shirt, about the 1994 genocide by Hutu troops, Interahamwe militiamen and mobs and they deny it ever happened.
"It was a war, not genocide. We left Rwanda then because of war and we left Zaire now because of war," says Alphonse, a farmer from near the capital Kigali.
"Hutus and Tutsis are the same. We are brothers. There is no need for revenge by them."
"An international force is a good idea. We need help at home and seeds and money to recover from the war against us."
Asked what he would do if he found a Tutsi had taken over his home and the four goats and 10 chickens he left behind, Nitegeka says he would do nothing and find elsewhere to live.
"We just want peace, like the president says," he adds.
But as he speaks in Kinyarwanda, his two wives argue with him, not expecting a translator to relay their saying that of course he would fight for his home and his animals.
He says his time in eastern Zaire was not a waste, because his children are all alive, though the baby now has diarrhoea.
Asked whether he likes Vice-President Paul Kagame, the Tutsi former rebel leader whose war to end the genocide and take power led to the Hutu exodus, he says of couse he does.

The crowd around him clap feverishly at the mention of the name of Kagame, who was demonised by their former Hutu leaders and is widely thought by refugees to have been the mastermind behind the Zairean Tutsi rebellion which drove them home again.
